analysis.one_liner: Creates emergency border removal authority, speeds asylum decisions, and funds border agents, fentanyl enforcement, and Afghan allies.
analysis.headline: The Senate's bipartisan border deal failed the vote to open debate 43-50 on May 23, 2024, falling 17 votes short of the 60 needed, and never came up for an actual vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was the standalone Senate version of the 2024 bipartisan border compromise. It would give the government new emergency power to quickly remove migrants near the southwest border when weekly encounters top 4,000, make asylum officers decide cases on a 90-day clock with stricter standards, hire thousands more border and asylum staff, spend roughly $20 billion on border operations, detention, scanning technology, and fentanyl enforcement, and create new legal pathways for Afghan allies who helped the U.S. mission. It never advanced past a procedural vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Border communities and asylum offices would get thousands of new hires and faster case decisions; Afghan allies who supported the U.S. mission would get a path to stay; cities and nonprofits sheltering migrants would get $750 million in reimbursement; fentanyl interdiction would get new lab and scanning funding; border technology vendors and detention operators would get large new contracts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Border communities, Afghan allies, shelter providers

how_it_helps.text: Gives the Department of Homeland Security emergency authority to summarily remove or bar entry for migrants within 100 miles of the southwest border once weekly encounters average 4,000, with mandatory use at higher thresholds; the authority expires after three years.

Creates expedited, noncustodial asylum proceedings run by asylum officers with a 90-day decision target, work authorization for those who pass, and access to counsel, while cutting review of denied claims and raising the standard to stay in the U.S. pending a decision.

Expands immigration pathways for Afghan allies, including conditional permanent resident status for many who were admitted or paroled and more special immigrant visas for those injured supporting the U.S. mission.

Appropriates roughly $20 billion in emergency spending, including about $4 billion for CBP hiring, $6 billion for ICE detention, removal flights, and staff, $2 billion for scanning technology at ports of entry, $440 million for immigration judges, and new money for fentanyl lab analysis and enforcement.
Sends $750 million to the Shelter and Services Program to reimburse states and nonprofits that house migrants, and funds legal counsel programs for unaccompanied children and incompetent adults.
Raises asylum officer pay by 15 percent and grants temporary direct-hire authority to staff up the system quickly.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the roughly $20 billion in new emergency spending. Asylum seekers bear tighter screening standards, shorter timelines, and expanded emergency removal authority near the border.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers; asylum seekers under stricter rules

drawbacks.text: The emergency authority would let the government summarily remove migrants near the border without normal asylum access whenever weekly encounters top 4,000, and higher thresholds make it mandatory.

A denied claim under the new expedited track can lead to a removal order without hearing or review, apart from a request to reconsider, and the bill sets a stricter standard for staying in the country while a case is pending.
The bill waives the polygraph requirement that has applied to Border Patrol hires since 2010, allowing waivers for current local and federal officers and for veterans with clearances.
It expands immigrant detention capacity and removal flights, and all of its spending is designated emergency spending, which adds to the deficit without an offset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine two-sided compromise: faster, better-resourced decisions and real legal pathways for Afghan allies came packaged with sharply narrower access to asylum and expanded detention and removal. Honest supporters could argue the trade fixed a broken backlog; critics on both the left and right agreed with each other that the trade was bad, for opposite reasons. The strongest design concern is the breadth of the emergency removal authority and the limited review of denied claims.

outcome.mechanism: A vote to start Senate debate on the bill failed 43-50, well short of the 60 votes needed, so the chamber never debated or voted on the bill itself.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Murphy introduced the Border Act of 2024 on May 16, 2024, and it was placed on the Senate calendar two days later.
Senators took four procedural steps to reach the bill between May 21 and May 23, including filing a cloture motion on the motion to proceed, which is the vote needed to open debate.
On May 23, 2024, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 43-50; 41 Democrats and 1 Independent voted yes, while 44 Republicans, 4 Democrats, and 2 Independents voted no.
Because the vote to open debate failed, the bill never received a vote on its merits, and the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without it advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Neither side got a law: the border and asylum system stayed exactly as it was. The senators who voted it down avoided a recorded vote on the negotiated compromise, and the issue remained alive going into the 2024 elections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo and the senators who blocked it

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to bring it to the floor for debate.

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Co-negotiated the original bipartisan border compromise and was the lone Republican voting to proceed to this version.

for.name: Sen. Kyrsten Sinema
for.what_they_did: Co-negotiated the compromise and voted to proceed to the bill.

for.name: National Border Patrol Council
for.what_they_did: Publicly endorsed the underlying border deal, the first time the union had backed a major immigration bill.

against.name: 44 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted nearly unanimously against the motion to proceed, keeping the bill from debate and a floor vote.

against.name: Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against the border deal, and Republicans withdrew support after initially negotiating it.

against.name: Four Democratic senators
against.what_they_did: Voted against the motion to proceed, objecting to provisions they viewed as too restrictive on asylum.

sides.party_line_note: On the 43-50 vote to open debate, 41 of 45 Democrats and Independents voted yes while only 1 of 45 Republicans did, though four Democrats also voted no, mostly over asylum restrictions.

industries.note: The bill directs about $2 billion to non-intrusive inspection (scanning) technology, $170 million to autonomous surveillance towers, and $260 million to other border technology, awarded through open competition. This spending is aimed at detecting fentanyl and illegal crossings, which its backers cast as a public-safety benefit.

industries.industry: Private immigration detention and transport contractors
industries.note: The bill provides $1.67 billion to expand detention capacity and $2.47 billion for removal flights and staging facilities, money that flows to detention and transport operators. More detention and faster removals are the part of the bill that critics of the compromise found most costly to migrants.

industries.industry: Afghan allies who worked with the U.S. mission
industries.note: The bill creates conditional permanent resident status for many Afghan allies admitted or paroled to the U.S. and expands special immigrant visas for those injured supporting the U.S. mission, resolving an uncertain status left after the 2021 withdrawal.

The bill funds representation for unaccompanied children and incompetent adults, $440 million for immigration judge teams, and $750 million to reimburse communities and nonprofits sheltering migrants.
